Emergence of Diffusion Models from Associative Memory through Memorization and Generalization

Bao Pham*, Gabriel Raya*, Matteo Negri, Mohammed J. Zaki, Luca Ambrogioni, Dmitry Krotov
Nature Communications, 2026
*Indicates Equal Contribution
Paper arXiv Code Slides NeurIPS 2024 ICLR 2025

Generation viewed as descent on a Dense Associative Memory energy landscape. With little training data every minimum sits on a training example, and retrieval returns that example (memorization). As the training set grows, new minima appear between data points, which is the spurious phase. With more data still, the landscape flattens into broad basins whose minima are novel samples rather than stored ones (generalization).

Abstract

Dense Associative Memories (DenseAMs) are generalizations of Hopfield networks that store training data at local minima of the energy landscape. When the amount of training data exceeds the critical memory storage capacity, new local minima (different from the training data) emerge. These emergent local minima, known as spurious states, can hinder memory retrieval. We examine diffusion models (DMs) through the DenseAM lens, viewing their generative process as an attempt of a memory retrieval. In the small data regime, DMs create distinct attractors for each training sample, akin to DenseAMs below the critical capacity. As the training set size increases, DMs transition to generalization. We identify a critical intermediate phase, predicted by DenseAM theory, characterized by the emergence of spurious states. In generative modeling, these previously overlooked states are no longer negative artifacts but rather are the first signs of generative capabilities. Their existence is demonstrated across a wide range of architectures and datasets.

Highlights

  • Generation as memory retrieval. A Dense Associative Memory stores training data at local minima of its energy landscape. Reading a diffusion model the same way makes its generative process an attempt at retrieval, so the geometry of the landscape, rather than the architecture, explains what the model returns.
  • Spurious states are not a failure mode. Classical associative memory treats the minima that appear past the critical storage capacity as artifacts that corrupt retrieval. In a generative model they are the opposite: the intermediate phase they define is the first point at which the model produces something that is not a stored training example.
  • One transition, controlled by dataset size. Below the critical capacity, each training sample gets its own attractor and the model memorizes. Above it, the spurious phase appears, and beyond that the landscape flattens into basins that correspond to generalization. The phase is predicted by DenseAM theory and observed across a wide range of architectures and datasets.

Related Work

The discrete, token-level counterpart of this picture is developed in Language Diffusion Models are Associative Memories Capable of Retrieving Unseen Data. For the associative memory tools used here, see Modern Methods in Associative Memory and Energy Transformer, or my blog post on energy-based modeling.
